newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh alloys sees shining future after dark days.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh alloys sees shining future after dark days.

text.p: Kazakhstan, a major world producer of ferro-alloys, may see output jump this year as its main producer stages a comeback, officials said at the weekend.

"This year, Kazakhstan may produce 800,000 tonnes of ferro- alloys," Viktor Pirogov, director of the Aksussky Ferro-alloy Plant, the country's main producer, told Reuters. "This jump is realistic -- we have already concluded contracts for a sizeable part of this amount."
Kazakhstan's output of ferro-alloys, including those of chrome, was 548,800 tonnes last year.
Kazakhstan has the world's second largest chrome ore reserves, or 30 percent of the world's total.

The Aksussky plant, located in the steppe town of Aksu some 1,450 km north of the Kazakh capital of Almaty, is one of Kazakhstan's two ferro-alloy producers, accounting for over 80 percent of the former Soviet republic's alloys output.
Aksussky is part of national chrome company TNK Kazkhrom, whose main shareholder is British Virgin islands-registered Japan Chrome Corporation (JCC), which owns a 52.5 percent stake.
London-based metals trading company Trans-World Group, active in Russia's non-ferrous metals sector, finances some of the plant's operations and sells its products on international markets.
Ferro-alloys are essential to the production of high-quality stainless and heat-resistant steels.
Pirogov said that last year his plant produced some 500,000 tonnes of ferro-alloys out of the Central Asian state's total output.
"We could have produced much more, but world markets were glutted with ferro-alloys," he said. "We even had to close several facilities at our plant."
The activities of competitors also thwarted exports last year, Pirogov added.

"They tried to slash prices on our products by saying our plant would not be able to fulfil obligations on its contracts," he said. "But we have won the confidence of our clients and now have contracts for three to five years ahead."
The high-quality of Kazakh alloys was important, he said.
"Due to the unique composition of Kazakh ores, the quality of our alloys is much higher than that of our main competitors from South Africa," said Valery Matvienko, the plant's technical director.
Ferro-chrome makes up some 80 percent of the plant's output. Aksussky also produces ferro-silicium and silico-manganese.
The plant's directors were confident there would be no return to the dark days of 1993, when Aksussky's output plunged to less than 300,000 tonnes from 800,000 tonnes in 1989, its peak year.
"Before JCC and Trans-World turned up in 1995, the situation was just terrible," Matviyenko said.
He said Aksussky began staging its revival after foreign investors replenished the plant's working capital with an initial investment of over $80 million.
"When the reconstruction of five furnaces is over, and all 26 furnaces function, we can eventually achieve the level of one million tonnes of alloys a year," Matviyenko said.
"Many of our specialists, who went to Russia when the plant was in crisis, are now returning."
